name: Model Risk and Bias Testing
title: Model Risk and Bias Testing
answer: Model risk and bias testing covers the controls used to find, measure and limit harm from models that make or inform financial decisions. It spans credit scoring, fraud detection, anti-money laundering, underwriting, trading, collections and customer service automation. The scope includes the full model lifecycle, from data selection and feature engineering through validation, deployment and retirement. Bias testing sits inside that scope and looks for systematic differences in outcomes across protected groups or their proxies. It also covers documentation, explainability and the evidence needed to show that a model behaves as intended.

sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on a model inventory and registry that records each model's purpose, owner, version and dependencies. Validation and testing environments are kept separate from production, with controlled access and reproducible data snapshots. Common building blocks include data lineage and metadata tools, feature stores, version control, automated test harnesses and monitoring dashboards. Open source libraries such as Fairlearn, AI Fairness 360 and SHAP are widely used for fairness metrics and explanation, alongside commercial model risk platforms. Logs, test results and approvals are retained so that an auditor can reconstruct what was tested and when.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Practitioners start with a model inventory and tier models by materiality, complexity and potential customer impact. Independent validation then checks conceptual soundness, data quality, assumptions, implementation and outcomes against benchmarks or challenger models. Bias testing defines the protected attributes and the fairness metrics that matter for the use case, such as demographic parity, equalized odds or predictive parity, then measures gaps across slices of the population. Testers also look for proxy variables, label bias, sampling bias and feedback loops that can hide discrimination behind apparently neutral features. After deployment, monitoring, periodic revalidation and change control keep the evidence current.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk here turn on non-discrimination, explainability, data protection and the ability to challenge an adverse decision. In the United States, model risk expectations often trace to supervisory guidance such as SR 11-7 and to fair lending and consumer credit laws, while the EU AI Act and GDPR add duties around high-risk systems and automated decisions. Provenance matters because bias testing is only as good as the data lineage, consent records and documentation behind it, including model cards, version histories and audit trails. Failures can bring regulatory action, litigation, remediation costs and reputational damage, and the site's 219 compliance and regulation pages and 148 active AI lawsuits show how active this area has become. Good practice is to keep testing evidence, decisions and exceptions in a form that regulators, auditors and internal review can inspect.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward continuous, automated testing rather than periodic paper exercises. Generative AI and large language models bring new model risk questions around hallucination, prompt sensitivity, data leakage and unstable outputs, which existing validation templates do not always fit. Regulators are moving toward sharper expectations for third-party models, documentation and post-market monitoring. Fairness metrics are becoming more standardized, but the hard work remains in choosing the right definition for a given decision and defending that choice. Provenance, auditability and human oversight are likely to stay central as more financial workflows depend on models.
